stem: Calculate the mole fraction of ethylene glycol \(\text{(C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2)\) in a solution containing 20% of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\) by mass.
solution:
Assume that we have \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution (one can start with any amount of solution because the results obtained will be the same). Solution will contain \(20\,\text{g}\) of ethylene glycol and \(80\,\text{g}\) of water.

Molar mass of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = 12 \times 2 + 1 \times 6 + 16 \times 2 = 62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

Moles of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{20\,\text{g}}{62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.322\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of water \(= \dfrac{80\,\text{g}}{18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 4.444\,\text{mol}\)

\(x_{\text{glycol}} = \dfrac{\text{moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2}{\text{moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 + \text{moles of }\text{H}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{0.322\,\text{mol}}{0.322\,\text{mol} + 4.444\,\text{mol}} = 0.068\)

Similarly, \(x_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{4.444\,\text{mol}}{0.322\,\text{mol} + 4.444\,\text{mol}} = 0.932\)

Mole fraction of water can also be calculated as: \(1 - 0.068 = 0.932\)

stem: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing \(5\,\text{g}\) of NaOH in \(450\,\text{mL}\) solution.
solution:
Moles of NaOH \(= \dfrac{5\,\text{g}}{40\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.125\,\text{mol}\)

Volume of the solution in litres \(= 450\,\text{mL} / 1000\,\text{mL L}^{-1}\)

Using equation (2.8),

Molarity \(= \dfrac{0.125\,\text{mol} \times 1000\,\text{mL L}^{-1}}{450\,\text{mL}} = 0.278\,\text{M}\)

\(= 0.278\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(= 0.278\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.8)"; the molarity definition in this chapter is equation (1.8). Stale cross-reference left over from an edition in which this was Unit 2. Transcribed faithfully, not corrected.

stem: Calculate molality of \(2.5\,\text{g}\) of ethanoic acid \((\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})\) in \(75\,\text{g}\) of benzene.
solution:
Molar mass of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\): \(12 \times 2 + 1 \times 4 + 16 \times 2 = 60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{2.5\,\text{g}}{60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.0417\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of benzene in kg \(= 75\,\text{g}/1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1} = 75 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\)

Molality of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{\text{Moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2}{\text{kg of benzene}} = \dfrac{0.0417\,\text{mol} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{75\,\text{g}}\)

\(= 0.556\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

stem: If \(\text{N}_2\) gas is bubbled through water at \(293\,\text{K}\), how many millimoles of \(\text{N}_2\) gas would dissolve in 1 litre of water? Assume that \(\text{N}_2\) exerts a partial pressure of \(0.987\,\text{bar}\). Given that Henry's law constant for \(\text{N}_2\) at \(293\,\text{K}\) is \(76.48\,k\text{bar}\).
solution:
The solubility of gas is related to the mole fraction in aqueous solution. The mole fraction of the gas in the solution is calculated by applying Henry's law. Thus:

\(x\,(\text{Nitrogen}) = \dfrac{p\,(\text{nitrogen})}{K_{\text{H}}} = \dfrac{0.987\,\text{bar}}{76{,}480\,\text{bar}} = 1.29 \times 10^{-5}\)

As 1 litre of water contains \(55.5\,\text{mol}\) of it, therefore if \(n\) represents number of moles of \(\text{N}_2\) in solution,

\(x\,(\text{Nitrogen}) = \dfrac{n\,\text{mol}}{n\,\text{mol} + 55.5\,\text{mol}} = \dfrac{n}{55.5} = 1.29 \times 10^{-5}\)

(\(n\) in denominator is neglected as it is \(<< 55.5\))

Thus \(n = 1.29 \times 10^{-5} \times 55.5\,\text{mol} = 7.16 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}\)

\(= \dfrac{7.16 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol} \times 1000\,\text{mmol}}{1\,\text{mol}} = 0.716\,\text{mmol}\)

stem: Vapour pressure of chloroform \((\text{CHCl}_3)\) and dichloromethane \((\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2)\) at \(298\,\text{K}\) are \(200\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(415\,\text{mm Hg}\) respectively. (i) Calculate the vapour pressure of the solution prepared by mixing \(25.5\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CHCl}_3\) and \(40\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) at \(298\,\text{K}\) and, (ii) mole fractions of each component in vapour phase.
solution:
(i) Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2 = 12 \times 1 + 1 \times 2 + 35.5 \times 2 = 85\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = 12 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 + 35.5 \times 3 = 119.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2 = \dfrac{40\,\text{g}}{85\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.47\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = \dfrac{25.5\,\text{g}}{119.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.213\,\text{mol}\)

Total number of moles \(= 0.47 + 0.213 = 0.683\,\text{mol}\)

\(x_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = \dfrac{0.47\,\text{mol}}{0.683\,\text{mol}} = 0.688\)

\(x_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 1.00 - 0.688 = 0.312\)

Using equation (2.16),

\(p_{\text{total}} = p_1^0 + (p_2^0 - p_1^0)\,x_2 = 200 + (415 - 200) \times 0.688\)

\(= 200 + 147.9 = 347.9\,\text{mm Hg}\)

(ii) Using the relation (2.19), \(y_{\text{i}} = p_{\text{i}}/p_{\text{total}}\), we can calculate the mole fraction of the components in gas phase \((y_{\text{i}})\).

\(p_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 0.688 \times 415\,\text{mm Hg} = 285.5\,\text{mm Hg}\)

\(p_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 0.312 \times 200\,\text{mm Hg} = 62.4\,\text{mm Hg}\)

\(y_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 285.5\,\text{mm Hg}/347.9\,\text{mm Hg} = 0.82\)

\(y_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 62.4\,\text{mm Hg}/347.9\,\text{mm Hg} = 0.18\)

**Note:** Since \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) is a more volatile component than \(\text{CHCl}_3\), \([\,p^0_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 415\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(p^0_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 200\,\text{mm Hg}]\) and the vapour phase is also richer in \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) \([\,y_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 0.82\) and \(y_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 0.18]\), it may thus be concluded that at equilibrium, vapour phase will be always rich in the component which is more volatile.
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.16)" and "relation (2.19)"; in this chapter these are equations (1.16) and (1.19). Stale cross-references left over from an edition in which this was Unit 2 (the same slip as Eg 1.2). Transcribed faithfully, not corrected.
